name: Plausible
tagline: Open-source web analytics that collects without cookies.
description: Plausible is cookieless web analytics with an open-source build and a dashboard you can publish on a public link.
pros: The dashboard can be published on a shared address, so a report goes out as a link instead of an export with permissions attached.
Collection is cookieless and stores nothing on the visitor's device, which is why this repository's consent-management page records that no banner is required.
The server code is open, so an operator can read what the tracking script and the backend actually do before trusting either.
Install is one script tag, with no event taxonomy, tag manager, or release cycle needed to start recording visits.
The recorded band of $9-69/mo sits in ordinary subscription territory, and the file lists the pricing model as paid rather than per seat.
cons: The single page stops at site-level questions, so there is no cohort, funnel, or account view to move into when a figure needs explaining.
With nothing persisted on the device, cross-session identity is deliberately weak and returning-visitor detail is thinner than in cookie-based tools.
Running the open-source build yourself moves upgrades, backups, and uptime onto whoever administers the server.

features.name: Cookieless visit tracking
features.description: Visits are recorded without cookies or personal data, which is what allows an install with no consent banner.

features.name: One-line script install
features.description: A single script tag in the site's template is the whole integration, with no per-event code to maintain.

features.name: Public dashboard links
features.description: The current dashboard can be opened by anyone holding its address, with no accounts or exports involved.

features.name: Custom event goals
features.description: Actions beyond page views can be recorded as goals and counted alongside the pages they sit on.

features.name: Open-source server code
features.description: The code behind the tracking script and the hosted service is published, so its behavior can be inspected.

features.name: Self-hosted deployment
features.description: The service can be run on infrastructure the operator controls, keeping the traffic data on their own machine.

features.name: Source and campaign breakdown
features.description: Visits are grouped by referrer and by campaign parameters, so the origin of traffic is readable at a glance.

features.name: Paid band of $9-69/mo
features.description: This file records Plausible as paid with a $9-69/mo range and no tier detail beyond that figure.

content.title: Dashboard links you can hand out
content.body: Plausible's most distinctive habit is treating the dashboard as something you can publish. A shared address opens the current numbers for anyone holding it, which turns reporting into a link rather than an export with permissions attached. That model works only because the figures are site-level and carry no personal detail: there is nothing sensitive in a pageview chart to expose along with the URL. For an agency, an open-source project, or a team reporting upward, it removes the seats-and-permissions step that normally sits between a report and its audience.

content.title: The script and what it does not set
content.body: Installation is a script tag in the site's template, and the collection behind it is cookieless. This repository's consent-management listing records that Plausible needs no cookie consent banner precisely because it does not use cookies, while a cost blog adds that it collects no personal data at all. Nothing is written to the visitor's device, which is what keeps that privacy claim structural rather than a policy promise. The tradeoff sits in identity: with no persistent identifier stored, close cross-session tracking of individuals is not what the product is for.

content.title: Single-page reporting and its ceiling
content.body: The dashboard is one page, and the items below are what it puts on it. Each one is a site-level question: how much traffic arrived, from where, and doing what. The ceiling is deliberate. Plausible answers what happened on the site without accumulating the individual-level detail that would turn the same page into a privacy problem.
items: Page views and unique visitors for the current period
Entry pages and the routes taken through the site
Traffic sources, referrers, and campaign tags
Devices, browsers, and countries of origin
Goal and event completions counted against pages

content.title: Recorded price band and directory rankings
content.body: The record here has Plausible marked as paid, $9-69/mo, and that band is the only price information our records contain; no tier breakdown or feature gating appears anywhere. The repository's best-privacy-analytics page ranks Plausible first for teams wanting analytics without cookies and consent banners, quoting the same rating and band this file holds. Those directory rankings are generated from dataset scores rather than from any testing, so they describe how Plausible is filed here rather than how it performed against anything.

content.title: Self-hosting and the open-source route
content.body: Plausible publishes its server code, so the same product can be run on infrastructure you control instead of on the vendor's service. That option reframes the privacy question: the traffic data never leaves a machine you own, and retention becomes your policy rather than someone else's. It also moves the operational load, because upgrades, backups, and uptime stop being another party's job. Our dataset records Plausible as a cloud deployment and says nothing about the self-hosted path in detail, so its current shape should be checked against the project's own documentation.

content.title: Plausible against the other cookieless tools
content.body: Of the nine comparison records in this file, three matter for a shortlist: Fathom, Matomo, and Google Analytics. Two blog entries in this repository list Plausible beside Fathom as the cookie-free pair, and the split between them is posture rather than principle, since Plausible centers on a shareable dashboard and inspectable code while Fathom centers on a flat single-screen install. Matomo is the self-hosted option for teams that want control without running a server themselves. Google Analytics appears as the incumbent the entire category defines itself against.

content.title: Scope limits and the basis for this page
content.body: Plausible suits a site owner who wants a public number, a script install, and a file that never touches the visitor's device. It does not suit anyone who needs to follow a person across sessions or break traffic down by account, because the product's design declines that data. Our file scores it 4.6 from 2,160 entries; those are directory figures rather than measurements. The observations above are assembled from Plausible's published documentation and this repository's files, and the software itself was not run for this review. No compliance certifications appear anywhere in these records, so confirm them with the vendor.

faqs.question: Does Plausible really need no consent banner?
faqs.answer: This repository's consent-management listing says so and gives the reason: the script sets no cookies. Whether a banner is still required on your site depends on everything else that site loads, not on Plausible alone.

faqs.question: Can Plausible be run on our own server?
faqs.answer: The product is open source, so a self-hosted deployment is possible. This file, however, records only a cloud deployment and gives no detail on the self-hosted route, so check the project's current documentation.

faqs.question: How does Plausible differ from Fathom?
faqs.answer: Both are cookieless and script-installed, and two blogs in this repository list them together. The recorded difference is posture: Plausible centers on a shareable dashboard and open code, Fathom on a flat single-screen install.

faqs.question: What questions will Plausible's dashboard not answer?
faqs.answer: Anything about an identified person, an account, or a journey spanning several sessions. The product declines that data by design, so retention, cohort, and revenue questions belong to a different tool.

faqs.question: What compliance records does this dataset hold for Plausible?
faqs.answer: None. No certification appears in our records, so a compliance review starts with the vendor's or the project's own current documentation rather than with this record.

author: Marcus Rivera
learningCurve: Very short — one script tag and a single page; the only real learning is which questions the tool deliberately will not answer.
whoShouldUse: Site owners, open-source projects, and agencies that want traffic figures on a public link and a tracking script that never writes to the visitor's device.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams that need person-level or account-level analysis, or that require durable cross-session identity, since Plausible's cookieless design gives that data up.
